newsitem.title: DUBAI: Record Indian, Mideast gold demand seen in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Record Indian, Mideast gold demand seen in 1997.

text.p: Weak world prices for gold were likely to sustain strong demand for the metal from the Indian subcontinent and the Middle East, with record imports forecast for the region this year, analysts said on Sunday.
They saw imports into Dubai, the main distribution hub to the world's biggest gold consuming nation -- India -- at over 400 tonnes this year.
This compares with a record 350 tonnes in 1996, as reported by the World Gold Council, a producer group which seeks to promote gold usage.
The strong demand was lengthening delivery times from European refineries, traders and bankers told a conference on the gold market.

"This market is very price sensitive and demand is buoyant at the moment. We estimate in the first four months Dubai imported 200 tonnes. So for the whole year it could easily be 400-500 tonnes," said prominent Dubai trader Harish Pawani.
"In 1997 it looks like Dubai will import 400 tonnes plus," said Jeffrey Rhodes of Standard Bank London's Dubai office.

Pawani attributed his upbeat forecast mainly to price, but said a month-long shopping promotion in Dubai and more local jewellery manufacturing was also boosting figures. "The shopping festival added an extra seven to 10 tonnes."
Traders said the January doubling of the amount of gold non-resident Indians could take home, coupled with more liberal government import policy in Pakistan, were also helping demand.

Arif Lakhani, chief executive of Habib Bank AG Zurich in Dubai estimated annual imports of gold into Pakistan at around 80 to 100 tonnes. "Dubai shipped about 35 tonnes to Pakistan in the past year. Our estimate this year is about 60 tonnes."

Tony Warwick-Ching of consultancy CRU International expressed confidence too in Dubai gold imports this year. But he sounded a warning on growth in Indian offtake continuing apace long-term amid competing demands on income. "There will be increasing competition for the consumer dollar in India."
Analysts said much would depend this year on rains in India's monsoon season, which begins in June. "If it is a bad monsoon, if there is drought, then demand will slow down," Pawani said.

Johnson Matthey gold marketing manager Peter Ryan said current strong demand meant European refinery delays. "At the beginning of February demand from this part of the world meant we were running the order book at six weeks forward.
"That abated somewhat in March, but since the beginning of April we have seen a return to new demand. We are now three to four weeks sold out," he added.
Conference delegates said Dubai traders and their buyers in India were stocking up on gold at the current level of around $342 an ounce and were not waiting for a sharp drop to buy more.
But if prices did fall markedly, more demand must emerge. "If it goes to $325 then we will see big buying, but I don't think it will send prices rallying much," said one trader.

Pawani, whose company is one of the largest gold exporters into India, agreed: "If there is a stable environment in price or any further erosion, demand from India will continue to be good. Up to around $355 we still consider stable," he said.

Ted Arnold, metals specialist at Merrill Lynch said that longer term, "once India finally becomes a fully liberalised economy you may well find that India goes the way of China. If that happens, India will surely cease to be the sponge for gold and silver that never, ever becomes saturated."
